historical_timeline.summary: Began to feel a small pain in her breast.
Mastectomy without anesthesia at her home in Paris.
Wrote her account of the operation to her sister.
Died, more than 28 years after the operation.

claims.statement: Frances Burney was born in King's Lynn, Norfolk, on June 13, 1752.
Burney's mother died in 1762, when Burney was about ten.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No cause of death is given in the cited source.

claims.statement: Burney married Alexandre d'Arblay, whom she met in 1793, and her only child, Alexander, was born in December 1794, when she was 42. In April 1802 she and her son joined her husband in France, where they lived for about ten years.

source_links.locator: Paragraph 8, on beginning her Paris residence nearly ten years before

claims.statement: Burney was a novelist, diarist, and playwright. Her first novel, Evelina, was published anonymously in January 1778, and she published four novels between 1778 and 1814.

In her letter Burney wrote that about August 1810 she began to be troubled by "a small pain in my breast," heavy rather than acute, which increased week by week. She resisted examination for some months; physicians and surgeons then treated her for months without success, the hardness of the affected spot increased, and her right arm was kept from use for many months. She noted that the breast was not discolored and not much larger than the other.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Patient's own account of the onset and course. The contemporary label is the evidence; no modern diagnosis is inferred from it.

claims.statement: On the last day of September 1811, at her home in Paris, Burney underwent removal of the breast without anesthesia. The operation was performed by the surgeon Larrey, surgeon of the Imperial Guard, with other physicians and surgeons present. She was given a wine cordial beforehand, and she wrote that the operation, including the dressing, lasted 20 minutes and that she believed she fainted twice.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented operation that anchors the synthetic mastectomy. No statement by the surgeon or by her relatives is used.

claims.statement: Burney described the operation in a journal letter to her sister Esther, begun in March 1812 and finished in June 1812, nine months after the operation; she wrote that she dared not revise or read it, "the recollection is still so painful." The manuscript is in the Berg Collection of the New York Public Library.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The letter is the primary source for the illness and the operation.

claims.statement: Whether Burney's breast disease was cancer is debated. Her letter and a modern biographical source call it breast cancer, but no tissue was examined; a 2024 article argues that it was tuberculosis rather than carcinoma. She lived for more than 28 years after the operation.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation without pathology. The specific diagnosis is graded R and is not asserted as fact.
Record the death as a fact without detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate a palpable breast mass in a postmenopausal woman of 59 with diagnostic mammography, ultrasound, and core biopsy; complete receptor testing, extent-of-disease MRI, and germline testing; coordinate mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy under modern general and regional anesthesia; recognize and manage a postoperative seroma; and begin an aromatase inhibitor with the bone-health, lipid, lymphedema, and distress monitoring of the CMID breast cancer protocol.

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Burney returns two weeks after presenting with a right breast lump and a year of heavy, dull breast ache. The diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound twelve days ago showed a 2.4 cm spiculated mass at 10 o'clock in the right breast, BI-RADS 5, with normal axillary nodes and dense breast tissue. The ultrasound-guided core biopsy ten days ago shows invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, strongly estrogen and progesterone receptor positive and HER2 negative. The ache is unchanged and does not wake her. She has no bone pain, cough, headaches, abdominal pain, or weight loss. She saw Dr. Marsh of breast surgery this morning. She is frightened of an operation and has asked that every step be explained beforehand and that she be warned before anything is done; with that, she feels able to go ahead. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer that she knows of, but her mother died when she was ten and little is known of her mother's family.

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Burney returns three weeks after a right total mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy. The breast MRI before surgery showed a second 0.8 cm cancer at 7 o'clock, confirmed by MRI-guided biopsy, so with Dr. Marsh she chose mastectomy; she did not want reconstruction. The germline panel showed no pathogenic variant. She had general anesthesia with a pectoral nerve block, was told of each step beforehand, and went home the next morning. Her pain was 2 out of 10 by the third day; she needed no opioid at home and stopped acetaminophen at two weeks. A seroma after drain removal was aspirated once by the surgical team eleven days ago and has not returned. The pathology shows multicentric invasive ductal carcinoma, 2.6 cm and 0.8 cm, grade 2, with clear margins and 0 of 3 sentinel nodes involved. The recurrence score is 13. Dr. Marsh and the breast program's medical oncologist advise five years of anastrozole, with no chemotherapy and no radiation. She has a little numbness under the right arm and is doing her shoulder exercises. Her bone density scan this morning shows low bone mass.

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Burney is a 59-year-old woman eight days after a right total mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy for multicentric hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. Her surgical drain was removed two days ago, when the surgeon also gave her the pathology: margins clear and the three sentinel nodes free of cancer. Since then she has felt a soft, sloshing swelling grow under the skin flap below the scar, with tightness when she raises her arm. She has no fever, chills, redness, warmth, or drainage from the wound. Pain is 2 out of 10 on scheduled acetaminophen; she finished ibuprofen three days ago and has not needed any opioid. She is doing her shoulder exercises. She came in today rather than wait, asking to know exactly what would be done.

referral.question: Palpable right breast mass, clinically suspicious for cancer, in a postmenopausal woman of 59. Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound are booked this week, with core biopsy if indicated. Please see her once the results are available to plan surgery
referral.urgency: Urgent suspected-cancer pathway, within two weeks
referral.pertinent_history: A heavy, dull ache in the right breast for about a year and a firm lump she noticed two months ago. On examination a 2.5 cm hard, irregular, mobile mass at 10 o'clock in the right breast, with no skin or nipple change and no axillary or supraclavicular nodes; left breast normal. Last screening mammogram three years ago. Menopause at 51; no hormone therapy; one pregnancy, with her only child born when she was 42. Never smoker; little alcohol. No regular medicines; no known allergy. Family history limited: her mother died when she was ten. She is very frightened of an operation and asks that every step be explained to her in advance and that she be warned before anything is done
questions: If the biopsy confirms cancer, would you recommend breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy, and is further imaging needed before deciding?
How should her axilla be staged?

consultant_note.history: Mrs. Burney is seen at the request of Dr. Pell with a right breast mass found two months ago, after about a year of a dull, heavy ache in the breast. Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound twelve days ago showed a 2.4 cm spiculated mass at 10 o'clock, BI-RADS 5, with dense breasts and normal axillary nodes. The core biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER 95 percent, PR 70 percent, HER2 negative. She has no bone pain, cough, headaches, or weight loss. She is postmenopausal and well. She is frightened of surgery and asked to be told in advance of every step, which was agreed
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound images and reports; core biopsy pathology with ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67; Dr. Pell's referral and examination; today's PHQ-9 and GAD-7

exam.finding: Right breast: 2.5 cm hard, irregular mass at 10 o'clock, mobile on the chest wall; no skin dimpling or nipple change; biopsy site bruised. Left breast normal. Breasts small to moderate in size
No axillary, supraclavicular, or infraclavicular nodes

assessment.display: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, clinical T2 N0 M0, hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative
assessment.assessment: Early-stage cancer suitable for surgery first. Breast-conserving surgery with radiation gives the same survival as mastectomy when the tumor can be removed with clear margins and a good appearance. In dense breasts, MRI can show additional disease that would change that choice. Staging scans are not needed at this stage without symptoms
The axilla is normal on examination and ultrasound, so sentinel lymph node biopsy is the standard; axillary dissection is not needed unless the nodes are heavily involved

Germline testing is recommended for every patient with breast cancer diagnosed at 65 or younger. Her family history is too limited to be reassuring. A pathogenic variant could change the operation, so the result should be known before surgery

assessment.display: Anesthesia and her fear of surgery
assessment.assessment: Her fear is understandable and is best met by clear information. The operation is done under general anesthesia, so she will be asleep and feel nothing; a pectoral nerve block placed before the incision and an opioid-sparing plan usually give good pain control afterwards

recommendations: Bilateral breast MRI now for extent of disease; biopsy any additional lesion before deciding on the operation

If the cancer is single and can be removed with a good appearance, breast-conserving surgery with sentinel node biopsy and whole-breast radiation; if there is disease in more than one quadrant, total mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy
Germline multigene panel testing now, with the result before surgery

General anesthesia with an ultrasound-guided pectoral nerve block (PECS II), an enhanced-recovery pathway, scheduled acetaminophen and a short course of ibuprofen, and opioids only if needed; an overnight stay
She will be given the date in advance and a written description of each step of the day, and the anesthesia team will explain each step before it happens
If mastectomy is chosen, a plastic surgery opinion on reconstruction is available; she will decide after the MRI
At the pre-anesthesia visit, baseline arm measurements for later lymphedema checks; after surgery, drain care teaching, and shoulder exercises from the first week
After surgery, a recurrence score on the specimen and a medical oncology review to decide on endocrine therapy, and on chemotherapy or radiation if the pathology calls for them
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Pell by telephone today; the patient agrees with the plan and has a written summary of the next steps
consultant_note.follow_up: Breast surgery will review the MRI, any further biopsy, and the genetic result with her within two weeks and set the date of surgery, with a post-operative visit at one week for drain removal and pathology. Primary care continues distress screening and survivorship care
